BILL OF SALE (GENERAL PERSONAL PROPERTY)
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Lee

PARTIES AND ITEM SOLD
This is a bill of sale between Jordan Alex Lee ("Seller") and Morgan Lee ("Buyer") for the sale of the following item(s) of personal property: One Samsung 55-inch QLED television, model QN55Q60C, with remote and original box. Seller states that Seller owns the item(s) described above and has the right to sell them, free of any lien, loan, or other claim except as otherwise disclosed in writing to Buyer before this sale. The sale described in this document takes place on November 28, 2026, at which time Seller delivers possession of the item(s) to Buyer. This document is a bill of sale for personal property (such as furniture, electronics, appliances, or equipment) between two parties; it is not a form for transferring title to a registered vehicle and not a deed or other instrument for transferring an interest in real property, as described further below.

PRICE AND PAYMENT
Buyer will pay Seller a total price of $450 for the item(s) described above, payable by: _______________________________________________. Payment is due: ☐ in full at the time this document is signed ☐ according to the following schedule: _______________________________________________. Seller's signature below, once payment is made as agreed, acknowledges receipt of that payment and transfers Seller's ownership interest in the item(s) to Buyer.

IMPLIED WARRANTY OF MERCHANTABILITY AND WHETHER IT APPLIES TO THIS SALE
California's enactment of UCC Article 2 (Cal. Com. Code §§ 2101-2328) implies certain warranties in a contract for the sale of goods, but the implied warranty of merchantability is not automatic for every sale. Com. Code § 2314(1) implies a warranty that the goods are merchantable in a contract for their sale only “if the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind.” Com. Code § 2104(1) defines “merchant” as a person who “deals in goods of the kind” involved or who, by occupation, “holds himself out as having knowledge or skill peculiar to the practices or goods involved in the transaction.” A private individual selling One Samsung 55-inch QLED television, model QN55Q60C, with remote and original box as a one-time, personal sale, rather than as part of a business of dealing in that kind of goods, is generally not acting as a “merchant” with respect to that item under this definition — meaning § 2314's implied warranty of merchantability generally does not arise from a sale like this one in the first place, independent of any as-is language addressed elsewhere in this document. A separate warranty — that Seller's title to the item is good and its transfer rightful — is addressed by Com. Code § 2312 and is not limited to merchant sellers; it can attach to a private sale unless excluded by its own terms or by circumstances indicating Seller does not claim full title.

  "Unless excluded or modified (Section 2316), a warranty that the goods shall be merchantable is implied in a contract for their sale if the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind."
  — Cal. Com. Code § 2314(1) (law.onecle.com reproduction), California Commercial Code, implied warranty of merchantability is conditioned on the seller being a merchant (https://law.onecle.com/california/commercial/2314.html)
  "“Merchant” means a person who deals in goods of the kind or otherwise by his occupation holds himself out as having knowledge or skill peculiar to the practices or goods involved in the transaction or to whom such knowledge or skill may be attributed by his employment of an agent or broker or other intermediary who by his occupation holds himself out as having such knowledge or skill."
  — Cal. Com. Code § 2104(1) (law.onecle.com reproduction), California Commercial Code, definition of “merchant” (https://law.onecle.com/california/commercial/2104.html)
  "(1) Subject to subdivision (2) there is in a contract for sale a warranty by the seller that (a) The title conveyed shall be good, and its transfer rightful; and (b) The goods shall be delivered free from any security interest or other lien or encumbrance of which the buyer at the time of contracting has no knowledge. (2) A warranty under subdivision (1) will be excluded or modified only by specific language or by circumstances which give the buyer reason to know that the person selling does not claim title in himself or that he is purporting to sell only such right or title as he or a third person may have."
  — Cal. Com. Code § 2312(1)-(2) (law.onecle.com reproduction), California Commercial Code, warranty of title is not limited to merchant sellers (https://law.onecle.com/california/commercial/2312.html)

Where a specific seller actually falls on that line is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve: someone who routinely resells a particular category of goods (for example, on an online marketplace) could cross into “merchant” status for that category even without a formal business license, and no case law construing that line for a casual or occasional private seller is cited here. Code § 2315's separate implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose, which turns on different facts (whether the seller had reason to know of a particular purpose and the buyer relied on the seller's skill or judgment) and is not analyzed in this document. AS-IS CONDITION STATEMENT
☐ Buyer is purchasing the item(s) described above AS IS, WITH ALL FAULTS, and Seller makes no warranty, express or implied, as to the item's condition, quality, or fitness for any particular purpose, except for Seller's statement of ownership above.
☐ Seller makes the following specific statement(s) about the item's condition, in addition to or instead of an as-is sale: _______________________________________________.

Buyer has had the opportunity to inspect the item(s), or has chosen not to, before completing this sale, and purchases the item(s) based on that inspection (or decision not to inspect) and Buyer's own judgment of their condition, rather than on any representation by Seller beyond what is checked above.

WHAT MAKES AN “AS IS” STATEMENT EFFECTIVE UNDER CALIFORNIA LAW
California law sets specific conditions for a seller's attempt to disclaim implied warranties, and “as is” language is treated differently from a general disclaimer. Com. Code § 2316(2) provides that, to exclude the implied warranty of merchantability, the disclaiming language generally “must mention merchantability and in case of a writing must be conspicuous.” That general rule is expressly made “subject to subdivision (3),” which supplies a separate, narrower path: under § 2316(3)(a), “unless the circumstances indicate otherwise, all implied warranties are excluded by expressions like ‘as is,’ ‘with all faults’ or other language which in common understanding calls the buyer's attention to the exclusion of warranties and makes plain that there is no implied warranty.” In other words, the statute treats a plain “as is” or “with all faults” statement as its own, separately sufficient way to exclude the implied warranties § 2316 reaches, without needing to separately spell out the word “merchantability” the way subdivision (2)'s general rule otherwise requires.

  "Unless the circumstances indicate otherwise, all implied warranties are excluded by expressions like “as is,” “with all faults” or other language which in common understanding calls the buyer’s attention to the exclusion of warranties and makes plain that there is no implied warranty"
  — Cal. Com. Code § 2316(3)(a) (law.onecle.com reproduction), California Commercial Code, “as is” / “with all faults” as a separate basis for excluding implied warranties (https://law.onecle.com/california/commercial/2316.html)
  "A warranty under subdivision (1) will be excluded or modified only by specific language or by circumstances which give the buyer reason to know that the person selling does not claim title in himself or that he is purporting to sell only such right or title as he or a third person may have."
  — Cal. Com. Code § 2312(2) (law.onecle.com reproduction), California Commercial Code, the title warranty has its own, separately worded exclusion standard (https://law.onecle.com/california/commercial/2312.html)

NOT FOR VEHICLE TITLES OR REAL PROPERTY
This document is a general bill of sale for personal property such as furniture, electronics, appliances, or equipment. It is not a vehicle title-transfer form and does not satisfy California's separate statutory requirements for transferring title to a registered vehicle, and it is not a deed or other instrument for transferring an interest in real property. For a registered vehicle, Veh. Code § 5600(a) provides that no transfer of title or interest in the vehicle passes, and an attempted transfer is not effective, until the certificate of ownership has been properly endorsed and delivered and submitted (with the required fee) to the Department of Motor Vehicles, or the parties complete the statute's other listed method. Separately, Veh. Code § 5900(a) requires the selling owner to notify the Department of the sale within five calendar days, including the date of sale and the names and addresses of the owner and the transferee. Neither of those vehicle-specific statutory steps is performed by signing this document.

  — Cal. Veh. Code § 5600(a) (law.onecle.com reproduction), California Vehicle Code, a vehicle title transfer requires DMV-directed endorsement and delivery of the certificate of ownership (https://law.onecle.com/california/vehicle/5600.html)
  "Whenever the owner of a vehicle registered under this code sells or transfers his or her title or interest in, and delivers the possession of, the vehicle to another, the owner shall, within five calendar days, notify the department of the sale or transfer giving the date thereof, the name and address of the owner and of the transferee, and the description of the vehicle that is required in the appropriate form provided for that purpose by the department."
